newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Telematics seen a way to tackle Euro road snarlups.
newsitem.headline: Telematics seen a way to tackle Euro road snarlups.

text.p: Telematics, the combination of telecommunications technology with information systems, is one tool European countries can use to help defeat traffic congestion as transport demand surges ahead of network expansion in the early part of the next century.

Klaus Rehder, substitute member of the European Parliament's committee on transport and tourism told delegates to a transport conference on Tuesday that telematics was being examined as a way of improving safety, traffic flows and reducing emissions.
The three-day European Market for Infrastructural Projects conference is discussing European telecoms and transport issues.

"We are sure that telematics advances must be taken into consideration in decisions on trans-European networks and stress that possibilities for bringing about a shift in traffic by means of telematics must be explored as well," Rehder said.
Telematics allows road users to avoid congestion, pointing out alternative routes, while freight companies can keep closer tabs on their trucks with positioning equipment.

The technology could have an important role to play soon as EU Commission forecasts see a doubling in transport demand by the year 2010 and only modest expansion of existing networks, said Rehder. "Other forecasts see even faster growth than that."

Rehder told delegates the Commission was proposing to develop a European rail traffic management which involved neighbouring countries and proposed telematic applications for 2,000 km of the busiest European highways and 10 cities.
"A modest 10 percent decrease in road traffic congestion would bring cost savings of 10 billion ECUs a year," he said.

The European Parliament was calling on the Commission to encourage private investment into telematics and even though the sector might be shy, the parliament was proposing to consider ways of using telematics in controlling police, fire and other emergency services vehicles.

But large-scale telematics could not be introduced overnight. "Data networks need to be expanded and powerful low-cost computers must be developed and linked in networks," Rehder said, pointing out that only a limited number of transmission frequencies were currently available.
Apart from health and safety issues related to electro magnetic radiation and driver distraction, attention should be drawn to data protection, Rehder said.
"There must be no possibility that personal data or movement patterns might be recorded outside users' control in a form that could be stored," he told the conference.

"I am sure when all these proposals and questions have been treated, telematics can contribute to a more intelligent use of infrastructure. New and additional efforts in telematics are worthwhile and will point the way ahead for the future," he said. -- Keiron Henderson, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
